concepts.title: Generalization
concepts.one_liner: One desired property of any vision system is its ability to generalize outside of the domain for which it was designed to operate.
concepts.content: One desired property of any vision system is its ability to generalize outside of the domain for which it was designed to operate. In the approach presented in this chapter, the domain of images the algorithm is expected to work on is defined by the assumptions described in . Later in the book, when we describe learning-based approaches, the training dataset will specify the domain. What happens when assumptions are violated? Or when the images contain configurations that we did not consider while designing the algorithm?
concepts.motivation_md: Generalization is crucial because vision systems often encounter images or scenarios beyond their original design assumptions, and we want them to still perform well.
concepts.recap_md:

- The domain is defined by assumptions or training data.
- Violations of assumptions challenge system performance.

concepts.title: impossible steps
concepts.one_liner: The impossible steps figure shows a shape that looks rectangular on one side and stepped on the other, illustrating ambiguous 3D perception.
concepts.content:
@fig-impossible shows the impossible steps inspired from @Adelson99. On the left side, this shape looks rectangular and the stripes appear to be painted on the surface. On the right side, the shape looks as though it has steps, with the stripes corresponding to shading due to the surface orientation. In the middle, the shape is ambiguous. @fig-impossible shows the reconstructed 3D scene for this unlikely image. The system has tried to approximate the constraints, but for this shape it is not possible to exactly satisfy all the constraints.

concepts.title: Generic View and Nonaccidental Scene Properties
concepts.one_liner: There are a number of properties that will remain invariant and can help us in interpreting the image.
concepts.content:
Despite losing much information when projecting world coordinates to image coordinates, several properties remain invariant and help interpret the image. These include:

- Collinearity: a straight 3D line projects into a straight line in the image.

- Cotermination: if multiple 3D lines terminate at the same point, their projections also terminate at a common point.

- Smoothness: a smooth 3D curve projects into a smooth 2D curve.

[FIGURE:b2cd80b67cc832bd | A diagram illustrating two nonaccidental properties in computer vision. The top half, labeled 'Collinearity', shows two separate line segments that lie on the same straight path. The bottom half...]

Note that these invariances describe the projection from world to image coordinates; the reverse is not always true. For example, a straight line in the image might correspond to a curved 3D line aligned to appear straight, or two lines intersecting in the image might be disjoint in 3D.

Some of these properties, while not always true, can reliably infer aspects of the 3D world from a single 2D image. For instance, if two lines coterminate in the image, it is very likely they also touch in 3D, since otherwise a precise alignment would be required for them to appear coterminate.

These properties are called nonaccidental properties because they appear in the image only if they exist in the world or due to accidental alignments between the observer and scene structures. Under a generic view, nonaccidental properties will be...
concepts.motivation_md: These invariant properties help interpret 3D structure from 2D images by identifying reliable cues unaffected by viewpoint changes.

- Cotermination: 3D lines ending together project to 2D lines ending together.
- Nonaccidental properties help infer 3D structure from 2D images.

concepts.title: Vertical and horizontal 3D edges under generic view assumption
aliases: vertical and horizontal 3D edges under generic view assumption
concepts.one_liner: Vertical 3D lines project into vertical 2D lines in the image under generic views.
concepts.content:
In a simple world where all 3D edges are either vertical or horizontal, under parallel projection with the camera's horizontal axis parallel to the ground, vertical 3D lines project into vertical 2D lines in the image. Conversely, horizontal lines generally project into oblique lines. Therefore, any vertical line in the image can be assumed to be vertical in the world.

However, this assumption does not always hold. For example, a particular viewpoint can make a horizontal line project as vertical, requiring an accidental alignment between the cube and the observer's line of sight. Such accidental alignments are weak properties and can occur, so more general algorithms must account for them. For this chapter, only images with generic views are considered.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept helps infer 3D edge orientation from 2D image lines by assuming typical observer viewpoints, simplifying 3D interpretation.
concepts.recap_md:
- Vertical 3D lines project to vertical 2D lines under parallel projection.
- Horizontal 3D lines generally project to oblique 2D lines.
- Accidental alignments can violate these assumptions.

Conversely, horizontal lines will, in general, project into oblique lines. Therefore, we can assume than any vertical line in the image is also a vertical line in the world.

concepts.title: parallel projection
concepts.one_liner: Parallel (orthographic) projection is an image formation model where light rays travel parallel and perpendicular to the camera plane.
concepts.content: One of the simplest forms of projection is **parallel** (or **orthographic**) **projection**. In this image formation model, the light rays travel parallel to each other and perpendicular to the camera plane. This type of projection produces images in which objects do not change size as they move closer or farther from the camera, and parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image. This is different from the perspective projection, to be discussed in , where the image is formed by the convergence of the light rays into a single point (focal point).
concepts.motivation_md: Parallel projection simplifies image formation by preserving object size and parallelism, useful for certain vision tasks and modeling.
concepts.recap_md:
- Parallel projection involves light rays traveling parallel and perpendicular to the camera plane.
- Objects do not change size with distance in this projection.
- Parallel lines in 3D remain parallel in the 2D image.

concepts.title: image edges

position.section_title: From Images to Edges and Useful Features

concepts.one_liner: We classify image edges according to their most probable cause: object boundaries, changes in surface orientation, and shadow edges.
concepts.content:
One of the tasks that we will solve first is to classify image edges according to their most probable cause. We use the following classification of image boundaries (@fig-edgeLabeling):

- Object boundaries: These indicate pixels that delineate the boundaries of any object. Boundaries between objects generally correspond to changes in surface color, texture, and orientation.

- Changes in surface orientation: These indicate locations where there are strong image variations due to changes in the surface orientations. A change in surface orientation produces changes in the image intensity because intensity is a function of the angle between the surface and the incident light.

- Shadow edges: This can be harder than it seems. In this simple world, shadows are soft, creating slow transitions between dark and light.

We also consider two types of object boundaries:

- Contact edges: This is a boundary between two objects that are in physical contact. Therefore, there is no depth discontinuity.

- Occlusion boundaries: Occlusion boundaries happen when an object is partially in front of another. Occlusion boundaries generally produce depth discontinuities. In this simple world, we position the objects so they do not occlude each other but they will occlude the background.

concepts.one_liner: The gradient of an image at one location measures the direction and magnitude of intensity variation.
concepts.content:
If we think of the image \( \ell (x,y) \) as a function of two (continuous) variables (@fig-imageAsSurface), we can measure the degree of variation using the gradient: 

$$\begin{aligned}
\nabla \ell = \left( \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial y} \right)
\end{aligned}$$

The direction of the gradient indicates the direction in which the variation of intensities is larger. If we are on top of an edge, the direction of larger variation will be in the direction perpendicular to the edge.

concepts.one_liner: From the image gradient, edge strength is the gradient magnitude and edge orientation is perpendicular to the gradient direction.

concepts.recap_md:

\end{aligned}$$ The edge strength is the gradient
magnitude, and the edge orientation is perpendicular to the gradient
direction.

concepts.title: Figure/Ground Segmentation
concepts.one_liner: Figure/ground segmentation divides an image into foreground objects and background, a classical problem introduced by Gestalt psychology.
concepts.content:
Segmentation of an image into figure and ground is a classical problem in human perception and computer vision that was introduced by Gestalt psychology.

In this simple world, deciding when a pixel belongs to one of the foreground objects or to the background can be decided by simply looking at the color values of each pixel. Bright pixels that have low saturation (similar values of the red-blue-green [RBG] components) correspond to the white ground plane, and the rest of the pixels are likely to belong to the colored blocks that compose our simple world. In general, the problem of image segmentation into distinct objects is a very challenging task.
concepts.motivation_md: Figure/ground segmentation helps separate objects from background in images, a fundamental step in understanding and interpreting visual scenes.

- It was introduced by Gestalt psychology.
- Simple color cues can help distinguish foreground from background in some cases.

concepts.title: Planarity constraints for flat image regions
concepts.one_liner: Flat image regions impose planarity constraints requiring the second derivatives of $Y$ to be zero: $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 = 0$, $\partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 = 0$, and $\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x = 0$.
concepts.content:
We assume that object faces are planar. Thus, flat image regions impose the following constraints on the local 3D structure:

$$\begin{aligned}
\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 &= 0  \\
\partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 &= 0 \\
\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x &= 0 
\end{aligned}$$

That is, the second order derivatives of $Y$ should be zero.
concepts.motivation_md: Planarity constraints enforce that flat regions correspond to planar surfaces by requiring zero second derivatives of $Y$.
concepts.recap_md:
- Flat regions imply planar surfaces.
- Planarity means $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 = \partial^2 Y / \partial y^2 = \partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x = 0$.
- Second derivatives of $Y$ vanish in flat regions.

slots.motivation: Planarity constraints enforce that flat regions correspond to planar surfaces by requiring zero second derivatives of $Y$.

\partial^2 Y / \partial y \partial x &= 0 
\end{aligned}$$

concepts.title: Approximation of second order derivatives for planarity constraints
concepts.one_liner: Second order derivatives can be approximated by applying first order derivative approximations twice, e.g., $\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y)$.
concepts.content:
The second order derivatives are zero as stated. To approximate these continuous partial derivatives, we apply the first order derivative approximations twice (as given by equations (@eq-image_partial_derivatives_aprox)). The result is:

$$\partial^2 Y / \partial x^2 \simeq 2Y(x,y)-Y(x+1,y)-Y(x-1,y),$$

and similarly for $\partial^2 X / \partial x^2$.
concepts.motivation_md: Approximating second order derivatives numerically allows enforcing planarity constraints on discrete image data.

- Similar approximations apply for $X$ derivatives.

concepts.title: A Simple Inference Scheme
concepts.one_liner: All constraints can be written as an overdetermined linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$ and solved by minimizing $J = \sum_i w_i (\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} - b_i)^2$ using the pseudoinverse.
concepts.motivation_md: Formulating constraints as a linear system allows efficient computation of the 3D structure by solving an overdetermined system.
concepts.recap_md:
- Constraints form an overdetermined linear system $\mathbf{A} \mathbf{Y} = \mathbf{b}$.
- Solve by minimizing weighted least squares cost $J = \sum_i w_i (\mathbf{a}_i \mathbf{Y} - b_i)^2$.
- Solution computed via pseudoinverse: $\mathbf{Y} = (\mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^T \mathbf{b}$.

motivation.text: Our formulation has resulted on a big system of linear constraints (there are more equations than there are pixels in the image).

example.text: For instance, if the index $i$ corresponds to one of the pixels inside one of the planar faces of a foreground object, then there will be three equations. One of the planarity constraint can be written as $\mathbf{a}_i = [0, \dots, 0, -1, 2, -1, 0, \dots, 0]$, $b_i=0$, and analogous equations can be written for the other two.
